client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother died six months ago. Every time my friends invite me out, I go because I think it'll help, but I just end up feeling hollow and disconnected the whole time, like I'm watching everyone else have fun through a glass wall. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up and try something new, especially when you're carrying such profound grief — and I'm truly glad you're here. That image of watching others through a glass wall is so vivid and telling; it sounds like part of you is reaching for connection while another part feels completely unreachable right now, which makes a lot of sense after losing your brother. I'm curious — when you're in those moments with your friends, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind about yourself or about what's happening around you?

client: It's like my brain just keeps telling me that they don't really get it, that they're laughing and talking about normal stuff and I'm just... somewhere else entirely. And then I start feeling guilty, like I should be able to just show up and be present for them, because they're trying, you know? But the more I push myself to act normal, the more fake it feels, and then I just feel even more alone than if I'd stayed home.
therapist: What you're describing makes so much sense — you're caught in a really painful loop where pushing yourself to seem okay actually deepens the disconnection and then guilt piles on top of grief, which is an exhausting weight to carry. That thought "I *should* be able to show up normally" is worth gently examining together, because six months after losing your brother, there may be a part of you holding yourself to a standard that doesn't leave any room for the enormity of what you've been through. I wonder — where do you think that "should" comes from, and whose voice does it sound like when you hear it?

client: Honestly, when I sit with that question... I think it sounds like my own voice, but maybe it started as my mom's. She always kept everything together no matter what, never let us see her fall apart, and I think I absorbed that as just... what you're supposed to do. But saying that out loud makes me feel guilty too, like I'm blaming her for something when she was just trying to be strong for us.
therapist: What a meaningful insight to arrive at — and it's so important to notice that recognizing where a belief came from isn't the same as blaming someone for it; your mom was doing her best, and you absorbed a lesson from watching her that made sense at the time. That belief — that strength means holding it together — may have served you well in other seasons of life, but it sounds like it's now working against you in your grief, essentially telling you that falling apart, even privately, isn't allowed. I'm curious, what do you imagine might actually happen if you gave yourself permission to *not* hold it together right now?

client: I think if I really let myself fall apart, I'd just... stay there. Like, what if I start crying and I can't stop, or I get so low that I can't function and go to work or take care of things? That's what scares me most — that giving myself permission to grieve means losing control of everything else I'm holding together.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and it's one of the most common things that keeps grieving people from letting themselves feel — this worry that the emotion is so big it will swallow you whole if you let it in. But here's something worth gently considering: you've actually been carrying this grief for six months already, and even in those hollow, disconnected moments, you *have* kept functioning — you've gone to work, you've shown up for friends, you're here right now. What if the feelings aren't a flood waiting to destroy everything, but more like waves that can move through you without permanently pulling you under?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but I think what scares me is that I've been managing by staying numb, and if I actually let myself feel it, I won't be able to put it back in the box. Like, right now I can go to work because I'm not really feeling it, you know? If I open that door, I'm not sure I can close it again and still function.
therapist: The numbness has genuinely been protecting you, and it makes complete sense that you'd be afraid to let it go — it's been your way of surviving something unsurvivable. And yet, I notice you're already feeling it in some ways — that hollowness with your friends, the disconnection, the guilt — which makes me wonder if the door might already be slightly open, and you're already managing more than you're giving yourself credit for. What would it look like to test this in the smallest, safest possible way — maybe allowing yourself to feel just a little, with some support around you, rather than facing it all at once?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible... but I'm not sure I even know what "a little" looks like anymore. Like, I've been numb for so long that I genuinely don't know if I can control the dial — what if I crack it open just a tiny bit and everything just floods in at once? And honestly, the idea of feeling that around other people, even with support, feels almost worse than feeling it alone.
therapist: That fear of losing control of the dial is so understandable, and it tells me how much you've had to work to keep yourself together — that's not weakness, that's survival. I want to gently notice something though: you've been sitting here with me, talking about your brother, your grief, your fear, and something is clearly moving in you right now — and you haven't flooded. What are you noticing in your body or your feelings in this moment, right here in this conversation?

client: I guess... I notice my chest feels tight, but not in the way it usually does when I'm about to spiral. It's more like something is pressing against the inside, like it wants out but isn't sure if it's safe yet. I don't know if that's progress or just me holding it together in a different way.
therapist: That description is actually really significant — something in you is already distinguishing between a spiral and this different, quieter kind of pressure, which means part of you is paying closer attention to your inner world than you've been giving yourself credit for. And I think that image of something "wanting out but not sure if it's safe yet" is your grief being remarkably wise — it's not flooding, it's waiting to know it's okay. What would it mean for this space, or even just this moment, to be safe enough for that something to exist, even just a little?

client: I guess... when you put it that way, it does feel like there's something almost careful about it, like it's not just chaos. But I'm not sure what "safe enough" even looks like for me right now, because I've spent so long just keeping everything contained that I don't really know what letting something out would feel like without it turning into a complete mess. It's like I don't trust myself to open that door even a little without losing control of what comes through.
therapist: It sounds like you've been the container for so long that you've lost touch with your own capacity to be with yourself — and that makes sense when holding it together has been the only tool you've had. What strikes me is that right now, in this conversation, you've been describing your grief with real precision and care — "something pressing from the inside," "careful, not chaos" — and that's not someone who loses control, that's someone who actually has a quiet, steady relationship with their own inner world that they haven't fully recognized yet. I'm wondering — if you could imagine one very small, private moment this week where you gave that "something" just a little space, maybe through writing, or sitting with a memory of your brother, what feels like it could be the gentlest possible first step?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that — that I have some kind of steady relationship with my inner world. But honestly, it also feels a little like you're being generous with me, like you're trying to make me feel better about something that's actually just... avoidance dressed up nicely. The writing idea, though — I've thought about it before, but every time I sit down, I feel like I'd have to do it right, like even that would become something I'd have to manage perfectly.
therapist: I really appreciate you pushing back on that, because that kind of honesty — noticing when something feels too tidy or too kind — is actually the opposite of avoidance, and it matters that you trust yourself enough to say it. And there it is again: that same voice that says you have to hold it together, show up normally, grieve correctly — now it's followed you all the way into the idea of writing, turning even a private moment into a performance you could fail at. What if the writing didn't have to be good, or true, or complete — what if it was allowed to just be a mess on a page that no one, including you, ever has to evaluate?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but I keep thinking... even if no one else sees it, I'll still know it exists. Like, I'll have written something messy and incomplete about my mom, and then it's just out there in the world, this half-formed thing that doesn't do her justice. It almost feels worse than not writing anything at all.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just said — you're not afraid of the mess for your own sake, you're afraid of not doing justice to your brother, of somehow failing him even in a private moment no one will ever see. That's not avoidance, that's love — and it's also grief, because when someone is gone, the things we make about them can feel like the only way we still have to take care of them. I wonder, what do you think your brother would say if he knew you were sitting here, six months later, still so worried about getting it right for him?
